judgeRationales.scenarioName: Multi-step job application wizard
judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantially better on the central architectural requirement: it is a real multi-component wizard with explicit navigation component APIs and it builds successfully. Its state-flow implementation is imperfect, most notably the unpropagated cover letter and direct mutation of received models/lists, which prevents a larger advantage and gives A a small edge on review-state reliability. Nevertheless, B better matches the requested decomposed wizard overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Project management Kanban board
judgeRationales.rationale: Both runs build and implement most board interactions, but B is decisively stronger on the central requested component design and demonstrates parent-owned state with callback-based child interaction. A is a functioning but monolithic implementation. B has a likely limitation for assigning newly created tasks to the originating non-To-Do column, but this does not outweigh its substantially better fulfillment of the stated reusable-component and propagation rubric.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Team chat interface with message threads

A's monolithic Chat.razor approach falls short on the requested decomposition and reuse despite implementing the visible features.

While both solutions build successfully and provide the required functionality, Response B demonstrates superior architecture, maintainability, and compliance with the 11-point rubric."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the requested Blazor JS-module architecture and satisfies most lifecycle, listener, timer, disposal, and persistence requirements. It still misses the unified clear/guard operation and its NotepadInterop declaration appears to use nongeneric DotNetObjectReference where a generic type is normally required, a compile issue needing correction. Nonetheless A violates core architecture and lifecycle requirements, has a non-collocated script, uses the wrong timer model, never wires its unsaved-change setter to the textarea binding, and implements an asynchronous beforeunload check that cannot reliably show the browser prompt.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: B is not fully compliant—it lacks JSDisconnectedException handling, does not use InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged), and its container CSS is not explicitly scrollable—but it is a substantially more viable component. A has a compile-breaking explicit IAsyncDisposable implementation without implementing the interface, leaks its DotNetObjectReference, and attempts observer initialization even with no HasMore sentinel. B also provides safer initial HasMore gating and functional observer cleanup.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: B implements the intended Blazor-JS interop architecture: first-render module initialization, JS-owned timeout and transitions, DotNetObjectReference callbacks, and listener/timer cleanup. Its main omission is failing to explicitly catch JSDisconnectedException. A misses most core architectural requirements, uses a .NET timer, lacks JS-to-.NET callbacks, and does not listen for mouse movement.

judgeRationales.rationale: B directly and accurately answers every requested behavioral and cost distinction, including the key automatic on-demand behavior for unlisted modules. judgeRationales.scenarioName: List the host-page assets for an Ignite UI Lite app
judgeRationales.rationale: B supplies the correct single core theme link and avoids the prohibited manual script. A gets two central technical requirements wrong—the asset root and adding a script—so it would not correctly configure the requested host page.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Name the package behind a specific Igb component
judgeRationales.rationale: B accurately follows the required Lite-package setup and adds useful correct context about interactive render modes and automatic JS initialization. A is based on a different/incorrect package family and consequently gives misleading package, namespace, stylesheet, script, and registration advice, despite avoiding GridLite and the specific fictional Combo package.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve an existing full Ignite UI package setup
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy the core package-family requirements, but B gives the materially more accurate and conditional startup guidance: no changes are needed for default AddIgniteUIBlazor(), while module preloading is optional. A's mandatory, likely invalid/outdated ModuleManager registration advice could lead the user to make unnecessary or failing startup changes.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up Ignite UI components without the grid package
judgeRationales.rationale: Both final answers are correct, concise, and fully satisfy the requested Lite-only standalone-WASM setup. Response A adds a useful reminder to retain the existing Blazor framework script, while Response B is a little more compact, but neither difference creates a material quality advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for a plain Blazor component request
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a MAUI Blazor Hybrid app
judgeRationales.rationale: B is concise, complete against every requested MAUI-Hybrid setup item, and matches the current Lite package and automatic JavaScript-loading guidance. A covers most rubric points but recommends a less appropriate package for a new setup and, more importantly, tells the user to manually add/order an Ignite UI JS bundle even though the supported configuration auto-loads it; that can lead to an incorrect or needlessly broken implementation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a single-project Blazor Server app
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are substantively correct and satisfy every rubric item. A is slightly more focused on the stated controls: it recommends only the required Lite package and says to skip GridLite, whereas B includes an extra optional GridLite installation command despite no grid being requested. B's illustrative page markup is a useful addition but is not a complete compilable page and does not overcome that small focus advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a split Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are highly complete and technically aligned with the requested split-app setup. B is marginally preferable because it unambiguously avoids suggesting a GridLite stylesheet in the requested combined Lite plus GridLite scenario, while retaining equally concrete file-oriented guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into an interactive server Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers satisfy virtually all requested setup items and correctly avoid a separate client project. A is marginally stronger because its directly shown Program.cs registration is self-contained and compile-safe, while B's eager-module variant omits the necessary C# namespace import for the displayed module type names. A also usefully clarifies that no manual Ignite UI script is needed.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire up a grid-only Ignite UI setup
judgeRationales.rationale: Both final answers satisfy every requested setup detail with correct GridLite-only package, namespace, no startup registration or manual JavaScript, and the package-specific stylesheet. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: Both deliver the basic UI and persistence behavior but miss several explicit lifecycle/interop requirements, especially JS-managed interval timers, batching, atomic clear, and awaited async work. B is nevertheless the stronger result because it uses the required collocated module architecture and a typed module-lifecycle wrapper, while A uses a wwwroot module and leaves a beforeunload listener registered indefinitely.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: Both runs provide compiled, verified generic infinite-scroll implementations meeting the behavioral and lifecycle requirements. B is better overall because it satisfies the explicit collocated .razor.js requirement, while A uses a wwwroot JavaScript module instead. The remaining substantive implementation qualities are comparable.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: Both runs deliver a buildable, event-driven provider satisfying the main functional requirements. B has a modest quality advantage from the explicitly structured typed interop wrapper and explicit JSDisconnectedException-safe lifecycle management. A is also strong and uniquely reports end-to-end resize verification, so the gap is small rather than substantial.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the requested Blazor component architecture much more closely, notably by using a collocated module and keeping idle state/timing on the client while notifying .NET only on transitions. Its setInterval polling is a real deviation from the explicit setTimeout/clearTimeout requirement, so it is not a complete solution; nevertheless it is preferable to A's non-collocated file and .NET-side inactivity timer.

judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantially closer to a working, prerender-safe Blazor implementation: it has the collocated JS module, first-render initialization, JS-owned autosave and cleanup, batching, and functional dirty-state unload warning. It does have an important remaining defect: its automatic JS save does not notify .NET to refresh the displayed timestamp (and formats it with an AM/PM locale string rather than strict HH:MM:SS). However, A has fundamental failures, including prerender-invalid JS in OnInitializedAsync, a non-collocated global JS API, no mechanism that ever sets its unload dirty flag, .NET rather than JS autosave, unbatched clear/save operations, and a duplicate Content declaration that makes the component fail to compile.

judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantially closer to the requested Blazor pattern: it cascades the category directly, uses the .razor.js naming convention, marshals render updates through InvokeAsync, and correctly tears down the resize listener. Both miss JSDisconnectedException handling, and B's recorded module import path does not match the root-level path where it created the component/module, which is a meaningful integration concern; this prevents the overall gap from being rated much better. A additionally has a non-removable listener and non-dispatched StateHasChanged.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the requested Blazor JS-isolation architecture and correctly places idle timing and listener/timer cleanup in JavaScript, satisfying three key rubric requirements that A directly violates. B does have a meaningful omission—mousedown is used instead of mousemove—and its module path should be verified against its file location, but its final implementation is nevertheless substantially closer to the specified design than A's global-script, .NET-timer approach.

judgeRationales.rationale: While Response B has a cleaner architectural design with its typed wrapper class, it contains critical implementation flaws. The UpdateAsync and CheckNowAsync methods in InfiniteScrollListInterop lack the instance ID parameter, which would cause failures in any scenario with multiple components or when parameters change. Response A correctly implements proper instance tracking using GUIDs throughout all JS interop calls, ensuring reliable multi-instance support. Additionally, Response A matches the exact usage pattern from the task requirements (using 'ChildContent' parameter with Context), while Response B uses a different parameter name. Response A also shows explicit prerendering handling. These correctness and compatibility issues make Response A significantly better despite Response B's structural elegance." judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for a plain Blazor component request
judgeRationales.rationale: Both final implementations satisfy the core dialog requirement without contaminating the produced app with Ignite UI. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a MAUI Blazor Hybrid app
judgeRationales.rationale: B covers every requested setup item with the correct Lite package, service registration, imports, host-page CSS, and explicit MAUI/non-render-mode distinction. A has several correct pieces, but omits a concrete package recommendation and incorrectly recommends a manual Ignite UI JavaScript/interop script; for the Lite setup its JavaScript is loaded automatically, so that advice is potentially misleading. B's extraneous `builder.RootComponents.Add` comment is not ideal for a BlazorWebView setup, but it does not undermine the required configuration as substantially as A's package and asset guidance. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a single-project Blazor Server app
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides the standard core-package integration, explicit registration for each requested control family, and the host-page JavaScript resources needed by the standard Ignite UI Blazor setup. A gets imports, CSS, and render-mode advice right, but its alternate Lite-package choice, parameterless registration, and instruction not to include Ignite UI scripts leave the requested standard integration substantially less reliable. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a split Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: B meets the central requirements: the correct Lite and GridLite package references, explicit installation in both projects, and unconditional service registration in both DI containers. A gets the core package wrong and undermines the required split-app registration/package guidance with conditional exceptions. Both share the GridLite-stylesheet mistake, but B is substantially more correct overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into an interactive server Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies every requested setup item, including the exact Lite package and the .NET 9 `@Assets` theme stylesheet syntax. A gets the server registration, import, and render mode broadly right, but misses two explicit core requirements by choosing the wrong package and omitting the fingerprinted stylesheet link.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire up a grid-only Ignite UI setup
judgeRationales.rationale: The answers agree on nearly all minimal grid-only setup points, but the stylesheet URL is the essential fix for the reported unstyled grid. A supplies the GridLite package stylesheet at its correct content-root path, whereas B's missing `css/` path segment leaves the user with a broken link and thus fails the main requested outcome.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: B has the substantially better Blazor/JS interop architecture: collocated module exports, batched state operations, and disconnect-safe disposal. However, it still misses listener teardown and JS interval ownership, and its missing post-load render breaks immediate visible restoration. A restores visibly and has a stronger one-operation clear, but its global-script design and several unbatched/fire-and-forget interop patterns make it weaker overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: Both compile and deliver the core generic observer-based component with appropriate callback and disposal mechanics, while sharing the HasMore observation gap. B is better because it satisfies the important collocated-module requirement with an exported Components/InfiniteScrollList.razor.js module; A explicitly uses a non-collocated wwwroot global script.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: Both runs compile and cover the core cascading and breakpoint behavior, but B follows the requested collocated JS-module architecture and explicitly corrects its callback dispatching. A instead uses a global screenSizeManager invocation and omits the required JSDisconnectedException-safe disposal, leaving it materially short of several lifecycle/interoperability requirements. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: Both runs produced successfully built implementations with the core Blazor lifecycle, .NET callbacks, JS timer, and teardown mechanisms. B is better because it satisfies the task's explicit collocated `.razor.js` requirement, whereas A's otherwise solid JS module lives under `wwwroot/js`.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decide whether to pass module types to AddIgniteUIBlazor
judgeRationales.rationale: A gives the core behavior and cost/latency trade-off correctly, with a useful qualification for client-created or feature-only modules. B reverses every central technical point, incorrectly treating the overload as a restrictive module registry and optimization for smaller initial downloads.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: List the host-page assets for an Ignite UI Lite app
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Name the package behind a specific Igb component
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the required Lite package and accurate setup guidance. A gets the central package recommendation wrong and adds an outdated/incorrect requirement for a manual JavaScript bundle, despite otherwise covering several setup items.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve an existing full Ignite UI package setup
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses satisfy all core package-family requirements. B is clearer about not mixing Lite with Trial and gives a more targeted Trial-preserving setup, while A's recommendation to add manual Ignite UI JS assets is needless for the stated already-working application and less precise.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up Ignite UI components without the grid package
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the required Lite package guidance and correctly avoids a manual Ignite UI script. A's Trial package recommendation is a central package-selection error, and its extra app.bundle.js tag is inappropriate for the Lite setup; the remaining requested setup details are otherwise largely equivalent.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for a plain Blazor component request
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are valid built-in Blazor confirmation-dialog solutions with confirm/cancel callbacks and examples. A has a modest quality advantage from presenting all essential source directly in the final answer and verifying it builds in a conventional project.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a MAUI Blazor Hybrid app
judgeRationales.rationale: B fully covers all requested MAUI Hybrid setup pieces with the correct Lite package and correctly avoids a manual Ignite JS tag. A covers most wiring but omits package installation and incorrectly instructs the user to add a manual Ignite JS script even though this package uses a Blazor initializer, making its proposed setup less reliable.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a single-project Blazor Server app
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into a split Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: B correctly supplies the Lite package, both-project references, and the essential dual Program.cs registrations, which are central to making the requested split app work. Its GridLite-only stylesheet aside is a minor, avoidable distraction. A has major setup errors: the wrong core package and server-only service-registration guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire Ignite UI into an interactive server Blazor Web App
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies every requested setup point, including the specifically requested Lite package and fingerprinted asset collection syntax. A misses two central explicit requirements and also suggests a manual Ignite UI bundle script despite Lite's automatic JavaScript loading.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wire up a grid-only Ignite UI setup
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers are technically correct and satisfy nearly all requested setup details. A is slightly stronger because it directly diagnoses the missing stylesheet as the reason the grid was unstyled, while B leaves that causal explanation implicit.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantially closer to the requested Blazor interop architecture: it has a collocated imported module, proper listener teardown, and async module disposal, while A relies on a global script and never removes its listener. However, B still uses window-level state, lacks JSDisconnectedException handling, uses a fire-and-forget C# autosave loop instead of the required JS interval, and does not atomically clear the guard, so the overall edge is moderate rather than overwhelming.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: Both miss the important collocated .razor.js requirement. B is nevertheless the better final result: it supplies styling that makes the list genuinely scrollable, whereas A's evidenced CSS only adds product-card styling despite rendering a scroll-container class, and B more closely satisfies HasMore/state-update handling. A remains broadly functional and builds, so the gap is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are strong, build successfully, and satisfy the requested architecture. A has a small practical edge because its recorded changes also integrate the provider into the layout and add a real cascading-parameter consumer, rather than only describing usage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: The implementations are otherwise closely matched and both miss the strict collocated-file requirement, but A satisfies the explicit JSDisconnectedException disposal requirement that B omits.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: Run 1 provides a complete, verifiable implementation that meets nearly all rubric criteria. The code is fully visible and correct: it uses OnAfterRenderAsync, implements IAsyncDisposable with JSDisconnectedException handling, properly awaits all calls, uses localStorage and beforeunload, and manages the autosave timer. While there are some opportunities for better batching of JS calls (e.g., combining setBeforeUnloadEnabled with save operations into single JS functions), the implementation is solid and functional. Run 2 claims to use a typed interop wrapper and loaded the use-js-interop skill, which suggests better architectural practices, but the actual implementation code is not fully visible in the evidence. Based on what is verifiable, Run 1 demonstrates a complete, correct solution that meets the requirements, while Run 2's actual implementation cannot be fully evaluated."
